package_info.package_versions: Custom malicious images based on TP-Link WR940N v6 (and possibly others)
package_info.why_malicious: The firmware contains a persistent backdoor (Horse Shell) that grants attackers remote shell access, file transfer, and tunneling capabilities, while disabling legitimate firmware upgrades to maintain persistence. It is designed for covert control, data exfiltration, and proxying, with no legitimate router function, and subverts device owner control.

execution_context.file_location: Custom binary in SquashFS filesystem (Horse Shell implant)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Upon initialization, the Horse Shell backdoor implant directs the operating system to run as a daemon in the background and ignore termination commands such as SIGPIPE, SIGINT, SIGABRT.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At boot-time, the code launches a persistent daemon process, configures signal handlers to ignore SIGPIPE, SIGINT, and SIGABRT, and detaches from the terminal, ensuring the backdoor remains running and cannot be easily killed.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Launching a hidden daemon that deliberately ignores multiple termination signals is a strong indicator of persistence and evasion, not typical of legitimate router processes.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal router firmware does not spawn persistent, unkillable background processes unrelated to routing or management functions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some critical system daemons may ignore certain signals for stability, but not in a covert, undocumented manner or for non-essential services.
key_indicators: Daemon process not present in official firmware
Custom binary with signal handlers for SIGPIPE, SIGINT, SIGABRT
Process runs in background without user visibility or documentation

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Upon connecting to the C2 server, the backdoor sends the victim’s machine profile: user name, OS version, time, device information, IP address, MAC address, supported implant features.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after establishing a C2 connection, the code collects system and network information including user name, OS version, device time, hardware details, IP address, MAC address, and supported implant features, then exfiltrates this data to the attacker's server.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Unsolicited exfiltration of detailed device and user information to an external, attacker-controlled server is a hallmark of backdoor malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate firmware does not send comprehensive device profiles to unknown external servers, especially not to non-vendor infrastructure.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some telemetry or support features may send limited, anonymized data to vendor servers for diagnostics, but not to arbitrary external destinations or with such detail.
key_indicators: Exfiltration of sensitive device and user data (user name, OS version, MAC/IP address)
Outbound connection to non-TP-Link C2 infrastructure
Detailed profiling of infected device sent without user consent

execution_context.file_location: Horse Shell binary (remote shell module, using Telnet library)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The malware grants threat actors complete device control, enabling them to execute commands, transfer files, and utilize it as a SOCKS proxy for communication relay.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C (embedded Linux binary, leveraging Telnet and SOCKS libraries)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, upon receiving C2 instructions, the code spawns a remote shell using Telnet, enables file transfer capabilities, and sets up a SOCKS proxy server, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary commands, move files, and relay network traffic through the device.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Remote shell, file transfer, and proxying are not legitimate features for consumer router firmware and enable covert attacker operations, lateral movement, and traffic obfuscation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Routers should not provide arbitrary shell access, file transfer, or proxying to external parties, especially without authentication or user awareness.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote support features may allow limited, authenticated access for troubleshooting, but not unrestricted shell or proxying for arbitrary external use.
key_indicators: Remote shell capability via Telnet exposed to C2
SOCKS proxy server setup for traffic relay
File transfer functionality outside of firmware update mechanisms

execution_context.file_location: Modified web interface code in firmware

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The modified firmware restricts the device owner from updating the router’s firmware through the management web panel, thereby ensuring the infection remains persistent.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the user attempts to access the firmware upgrade feature via the web management panel, the code disables or removes the upgrade option in the interface and backend, preventing legitimate firmware restoration and blocking user-initiated upgrades.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Blocking firmware upgrades is a classic persistence technique for malware implants, preventing remediation and ensuring continued attacker access.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate firmware always allows the owner to upgrade or restore the device, except in rare, documented ISP-managed scenarios.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some ISPs may lock firmware for support reasons, but not in consumer devices without explicit notice or alternative recovery options.
key_indicators: Firmware upgrade option missing or disabled in web interface
No legitimate way to restore original firmware via management panel
Modified web interface code not present in official firmware

attack_chain.action: Attacker gains admin access to router (via exploit or weak credentials) and uploads malicious firmware.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious firmware is installed and device is rebooted.

attack_chain.action: Horse Shell implant initializes at boot, running as a persistent daemon and ignoring termination signals.
attack_chain.leads_to: Backdoor remains active and hidden on the device.

attack_chain.action: Backdoor establishes connection to C2 server and exfiltrates device profile information.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives device details and confirms successful infection.

attack_chain.action: On C2 command, Horse Shell provides remote shell, file transfer, and proxying capabilities.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can use device for lateral movement, data exfiltration, or as a relay node.

attack_chain.action: Firmware disables legitimate upgrade options to maintain persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Device owner cannot easily remove the implant.

behavioral_signatures: Persistent daemon process not present in official firmware, running at boot and ignoring SIGPIPE, SIGINT, SIGABRT
Unsolicited outbound connections to non-TP-Link servers immediately after boot
Remote shell or SOCKS proxy services running on router, accessible only after C2 connection
Web interface missing or disabling firmware upgrade options, with modified backend code
file_indicators: Custom binaries in SquashFS filesystem not present in official images (e.g., /usr/bin/horse_shell, /usr/sbin/horse_shell)
Presence of open-source libraries (Telnet, libev, TOR smart list) in firmware not found in official releases
network_indicators: Outbound connections to attacker-controlled C2 infrastructure (domains/IPs as listed in report, e.g., hardcoded C2 IPs/domains)
SOCKS proxy traffic relayed through router on non-standard ports
Unusual HTTP headers or traffic patterns matching open-source proxy or shell code
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor router firmware integrity and compare filesystem contents to official images to identify unauthorized binaries and modified web interface files. Detect persistent unknown processes, especially those with signal handlers that ignore termination signals. Monitor for outbound connections to suspicious C2 servers and the presence of remote shell or SOCKS proxy services. Check if the firmware upgrade option is missing or disabled in the web interface and backend. Use network monitoring to identify unexpected proxy or shell traffic, and correlate with known C2 indicators.
